title: Hermes Consultant: Practice Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
Lesson 5 taught you how to map every stakeholder who can stop an implementation.
The opposite is true: lesson 5 taught you how to map every stakeholder who can stop an implementation.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
questions.explanation: Lesson 5 taught you how to map every stakeholder who can stop an implementation.

questions.question: Per the lesson about testing and verification, what is the central focus?
options: A history of testing software
A review of unrelated code tools
A summary of QA policy
The craft of proving an agent does what you say it does before you claim it to the client
questions.explanation: The lesson turns the claim-versus-result distinction into a method of watching tools fire and verifying results in the system.

questions.question: Per the lesson about kanban and orchestration patterns, what is the central focus?
options: A history of kanban software
A review of unrelated scheduling tools
A summary of HR policy
The three moves that keep a portfolio moving: scoping cards to fit a work window, dispatching to the right worker, and finishing with proof
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the coordination craft of turning a portfolio of work into scoped, dispatched, and proven cards without holding every thread.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the committed-to behavior when a client is affected by a live incident?
options: Go silent while you investigate so the client is not worried
Tell the client only after the fix is verified
Send short updates naming the observed failure, the investigation, the blast radius, and the verification target
Blame the model so the client knows it is not your fault
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the failure mode to avoid is going silent, and a short update that names the symptom, the investigation, the blast radius, and the verification target earns trust by showing work rather than claiming it.

questions.question: Per the lesson about automation and cron jobs, what is the central focus?
options: Turning a proven one-off win into recurring value on a schedule, with self-contained prompts and loud failures
A history of scheduling software and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson centers on turning a proven one-off win into recurring value, writing prompts that survive a fresh run, and making unattended work fail loudly.

questions.question: Per the lesson “What an Agent-Implementation Consultant Actually Does”, what is the central focus?
options: The agent-implementation consultant arc in one lesson: what an engagement looks like, what you actually deliver, and why this is not the same job as building agents for yourself.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The agent-implementation consultant arc in one lesson: what an engagement looks like, what you actually deliver, and why this is not the same job as building agents for yourself.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Installing and Deploying Hermes Agent: Local Setup, Profiles, Gateway, First Run”, what is the central focus?
options: The consultant's deployment discipline: how to stand up an agent correctly once you have the go-ahead. Isolation per engagement, a verified first run before you layer on features, and a gateway that turns a laptop experiment into an always-on tool your client actually uses.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The consultant's deployment discipline: how to stand up an agent correctly once you have the go-ahead. Isolation per engagement, a verified first run before you layer on features, and a gateway that turns a laptop experiment into an always-on tool your client actually uses.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Order the slices by convenience so the easy work happens first
A task that needs a reviewer to trust it is a sign to power through without review
Split a big goal by deliverable, apply a window test to each slice, and order the slices risk-first
One large task is better than ten small ones because it produces momentum
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches to split by deliverable, apply the 30 to 45 minute window test to each slice, and put the uncertain part first so its failure is cheap.

questions.question: Per the lesson about the finishing-the-job discipline, what is the central focus?
options: A tutorial on how to write better status updates
Delivering working artifacts backed by real evidence, reporting honest blockers instead of fabricating, and capturing what you learn
A review of unrelated project tools
A summary of corporate policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that clients pay for work, not descriptions of work, and that honest blockers are cheaper than confident fabrication.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: An installed skill is always current because it was written recently
A skill is a substitute for a capability the agent lacks
A capability is real only when you have evidence it fired, a tool call, an artifact, or returned output, not the agent's word
Trust the agent's report of its own work because it knows what it did
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a capability is real only when you have watched it fire, and skills rot so they must be verified against the live system.

questions.question: Per the lesson about MCP servers and integrations, what is the central focus?
options: Wiring an agent into the client's stack through MCP, deciding what it gets to touch, and proving the connection in the running system
A history of API standards
A review of unrelated database tools
A summary of network policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the three disciplines of integration: naming what an integration is, deciding the boundary, and proving the connection.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A loud failure is the worst kind because it makes the client nervous
Execution history alone proves the output was correct
A quiet failure is one that produces no error at all while the output is simply wrong
Stopping at it ran is enough because it is the important floor
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that quiet failures produce no error while being wrong, and are discovered by the client weeks in, which is the worst place.

questions.question: Per the lesson about governance and guardrails, what is the central focus?
options: A history of compliance software
A review of unrelated security tools
Writing an acceptable-use policy, treating PII as a bounded resource, and building guardrails that enforce the rules mechanically
A summary of marketing policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a capable, unattended agent needs governance as a design decision made up front, not a compliance checkbox.

questions.question: A consultant's weekly report renders perfectly and reports 41 open tickets while the client's data service holds 44. Per the lesson, what was missing?
options: An automated comparison of the report's numbers against the source
A better layout review before delivery
A larger model for the report job
A second weekly digest run to cross-check volume
questions.explanation: The lesson's worked example says the reviewer had opened the file, seen the table, and approved the presentation, while the missing gate was a comparison, the cheapest gate in the engagement.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: The reproduce doc is the one the client opens at two in the morning
A presentation that narrates your work proves the client can operate it
The runbook is the operate doc that gets opened in an emergency, and the evolve doc makes the client genuinely independent
Write all documentation from memory on the last day so it reflects the final system
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the runbook is what gets opened when the report does not land, and the evolve doc is what makes the client truly independent.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A tool tells the agent how to act the client's way, and a skill lets it act
The registry is a guarantee that all tools are available in every session
A missing skill means the agent physically cannot do the task
Availability varies by platform, credentials, and which toolsets are enabled, so treat the registry as a claim and the running agent as the evidence
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that ships with is not a guarantee of availability, so you answer capability questions from observed behavior.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The opposite is true: every few years a new technology creates a role that did not exist before.
Every few years a new technology creates a role that did not exist before.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
questions.explanation: Every few years a new technology creates a role that did not exist before.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The config file is always the value that runs, so precedence does not matter
Fallbacks only trigger on complete provider shutdowns and never cost anything
An agent with no fallback is fine because providers rarely fail
If you never verify what the running agent resolved, it works on my machine can be true for a reason you do not understand
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that precedence layers can override your file, so you must verify what actually runs, and an agent without a fallback is not dependable.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Large tasks are easier to report because they produce one moment of completion
A small task is reportable because honesty depends on knowing what actually happened, which is easier at small scale
A task that needs research and building is fine as a single piece of work
Slice work by activity, write the tests then the code then the docs
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a small task is finishable, verifiable, reportable, and has bounded failure, which is why it ships reliably.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist the reviewer not be the builder?
options: Because reviewing takes time the builder cannot spare
Because shared context produces shared blind spots, so the author fills in the missing step from memory
Because the builder is usually less senior than the reviewer
Because the docs forbid one agent from holding two roles
questions.explanation: The lesson frames independence as a context property: builder blindness is universal, and a reviewer sharing the builder's session, memory, and assumptions misses the same thing.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
The consultant lands in the client's world: their security rules, their existing tools, their network, their risk tolerance, their budget.
The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
The opposite is true: the consultant lands in the client's world: their security rules, their existing tools, their network, their risk tolerance, their budget.
questions.explanation: The consultant lands in the client's world: their security rules, their existing tools, their network, their risk tolerance, their budget.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Framing Value and ROI: How to Talk to a Buyer, Not a Builder”, what is the central focus?
options: The craft of turning what an agent does into a number a buyer can defend: how to measure value honestly, build ROI math that survives scrutiny, and talk outcomes instead of features to the person who signs the check.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The craft of turning what an agent does into a number a buyer can defend: how to measure value honestly, build ROI math that survives scrutiny, and talk outcomes instead of features to the person who signs the check.

questions.question: Per the lesson about security and credentials, what is the central focus?
options: A history of encryption
A review of unrelated antivirus tools
Storing secrets so they never leak, granting least privilege, and building guardrails that keep the client safe
A summary of finance policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the transferable craft of keeping the client safe across secrets, access, and guardrails.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Write the skill at the end of the engagement from memory to capture the final state
The description is the trigger, so name the situation it applies to, not just the topic
Skills should hold incident narration and ticket numbers so the next person understands the story
Any procedure that worked once, however trivial, deserves a skill
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the description is the only part loaded when deciding relevance, so it must name the situation the skill applies to.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Lesson 2 gave you the lifecycle and told you that discovery is not where the whole engagement is won or lost.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
Lesson 2 gave you the lifecycle and told you that discovery is where the whole engagement is won or lost.
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 gave you the lifecycle and told you that discovery is where the whole engagement is won or lost.

questions.question: In the review loop described in the lesson, what is the correct way to reject a candidate?
options: Block the card so the blocked column records the rejection
Reopen the task in triage for a fresh spec rewrite
Comment the criticism and let the implementer decide whether to act
Call kanban_request_changes with a reason so the review run closes as changes_requested and the card returns to the original implementer
questions.explanation: The lesson states that a block is reserved for real external escalation, and that rejecting by blocking burns the signal and drags the card into the block-recurrence path.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A guardrail relies on the agent deciding to behave
Hold the minimum personal data the work needs and retrieve the rest on demand, keeping raw records out of persistent memory
Write the acceptable-use policy after the build so it describes what you already built
Copy customer data into an external memory provider without asking the client
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the safest personal data is the data that does not exist in your system, so you hold the minimum and retrieve on demand.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A scheduled task that worked once by hand is a candidate even if it needed your judgment at three points
Automate a proven win, never a hope, and never schedule something before it works reliably by hand
Every recurring task should run as a full agent so it can reason
Script-only work is the right default for tasks that need judgment
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that you automate a proven win, never a hope, and scheduling before it works by hand just automates failure on a timetable.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The owner and the champion are the same person with authority and credibility
Authority alone spreads a tool and is enough to drive adoption
Adoption is measured by the number of features shipped to the client
You need both an owner who can say we use this now and a champion whose painful problem the agent solves
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that authority unblocks while credibility spreads, so you need both an owner and a champion to make adoption stick.

questions.question: Per the lesson on troubleshooting in production, what is the first move before changing anything in a live system?
options: Restart the gateway to clear the failure
Preserve the evidence (session logs, state, snapshots) so you can diagnose without destroying what you need to understand
Change the highest-risk config first to see if the symptom clears
Tell the client the fix is done so they stop worrying
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the most destructive instinct is to start repairing immediately, because the first action to fix often destroys the evidence you needed to understand the failure, so you secure the evidence first.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Training harder fixes most adoption failures because they are caused by ignorance
The old spreadsheet is the incumbent and always wins on default until using the agent is easier in the way the user feels
Mandate from a manager is the most reliable way to spread adoption
Adoption is a mass-market problem best solved with company-wide announcements
questions.explanation: The lesson argues most adoption failures are a fit or trust problem, not ignorance, and the incumbent habit wins until the new way is better where the user feels it.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on when each model fits?
options: Fixed-fee fits work whose scope you have done before and define tightly
Retainer is best for a one-shot implementation
Hourly fits work where the outcome is already clearly defined
Any model works equally for exploration, known outcomes, and ongoing operations
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches fixed-fee where the outcome is well defined and familiar, hourly where scope is genuinely uncertain, and retainer where there is ongoing operational need.

questions.question: Per the lesson on engagement models, what is the real decision behind choosing a pricing model?
options: Which model lets you bill the highest hourly rate
Which model produces a fixed monthly income
Who bears the risk of scope, and who the engagement model matches that risk to
Which model requires the least paperwork to invoice
questions.explanation: The lesson frames the engagement model as the contract over who bears the risk of being wrong about scope, and that risk split is where the money and trust live, not the rate itself.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson advises ignoring this entirely in practice.
Lesson 3 taught you how to find the real problem and write a problem statement the client agrees with.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The opposite is true: lesson 3 taught you how to find the real problem and write a problem statement the client agrees with.
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 taught you how to find the real problem and write a problem statement the client agrees with.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: It should work is an acceptable status to report
Fabricated numbers are fine as long as they sound reasonable
A plan that describes what the agent will do is a deliverable
An honest blocker is always cheaper than a confident fabrication, and a client would rather hear the real reason
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the worst failure is invisible fabrication, so reporting the actual blocker and reason is always cheaper and preserves trust.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Model and provider are the same thing and belong together in one setting
Secrets and settings belong in the same file so the config is easier to copy
Keep the model and the provider as separate keys so you can swap each independently
Verify a setting only by re-reading the config file you edited
questions.explanation: The lesson argues you must be able to swap the provider while keeping the model and vice versa, which requires keeping them as separate keys.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support about a retainer?
options: A retainer is a discount on a bulk block of hours
A retainer should name the set of included work, not just the hours it might cover
A retainer is only for the initial implementation phase
Under a retainer, your incentive is to bill for fighting incidents rather than preventing them
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that a retainer priced as hours in bulk is really hourly, and that a real retainer names the included work. It also teaches the retainer incentive is to prevent incidents so the system stays boring and the relationship renews.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Take a page, put the four groups on it, and for each one fill in three things: who plays that role in this client, what they need to be able to say yes to, and what happens if you do not win them.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.

The opposite is true: take a page, put the four groups on it, and for each one fill in three things: who plays that role in this client, what they need to be able to say yes to, and what happens if you do not win them.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
questions.explanation: Take a page, put the four groups on it, and for each one fill in three things: who plays that role in this client, what they need to be able to say yes to, and what happens if you do not win them.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Stakeholder Mapping: Who Has to Say Yes, and Who Has to Live With It”, what is the central focus?
options: The craft of mapping every stakeholder an agent implementation touches: users, owners, IT, and compliance. Who must approve the deployment, who has to work with it every day, and how to win both before you build.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The craft of mapping every stakeholder an agent implementation touches: users, owners, IT, and compliance. Who must approve the deployment, who has to work with it every day, and how to win both before you build.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Model choice is the largest cost difference in a long-running agent
The cache is the biggest cost lever because a mid-session model switch re-reads the whole context at full price
Switching models mid-conversation is always cheap
Inference is the largest cost of the engagement and should drive the price
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the cache is the biggest single lever, since a switch mid-conversation discards the cached prefix and re-reads the full context at full price.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Configuring a server is the same as connecting to it
The integration is only real when you have watched it fire against the live system on a real task
Hand your whole shell environment to the MCP subprocess so it has what it needs
A failed MCP tool call may safely echo a credential into the conversation
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the verification reflex: you do not trust the connection because you configured it; you give the agent a real task and watch it work end to end.

questions.question: Per the lesson about monitoring and observability, what is the central focus?
options: A history of monitoring dashboards
The craft of knowing when an agent is quietly failing, by separating loud from quiet failures and watching the whole fleet and the output
A review of unrelated logging tools
A summary of IT policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches observability as the ability to know what is happening inside a system from outside it, catching the failure no guardrail catches.

questions.question: Per the lesson about change management and adoption, what is the central focus?
options: A system nobody uses is a failed engagement; the craft of separating change from adoption and designing the agent around how people already work
A tutorial on marketing agent products
A review of unrelated time-tracking tools
A summary of payroll policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on closing the gap between delivering change and delivering adoption, which is where agent engagements quietly die.

questions.question: Per the lesson about tools and skills, what is the central focus?
options: A history of agent frameworks
What an agent can do comes from its tools, how it does it well comes from its skills, and how to know what is real in the running system
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of network policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the capability discipline of telling real capabilities from claimed ones and extending an agent without writing code.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Least privilege is a single configuration rather than a habit
Grant each agent only the minimum access required, with dangerous commands denied by default in unattended work
Approval is unnecessary because the agent will not misuse its power
The write sandbox limits convenience and is optional
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that least privilege is a habit applied at every boundary, and unattended work defaults to deny on dangerous commands.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Client specifics belong in the skill so it travels with all the details
Credentials belong in the skill file so the environment stays shareable
Never put a credential in a skill file, parameterize paths, and scrub client names so the asset stays shareable
A skill with no pitfall is the most valuable kind
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches to strip the client out: no credentials in the file, parameterize settings, and scrub names so the skill is a reusable asset, not a liability.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Discovery and Scoping: Listening Before Proposing”, what is the central focus?
options: The craft of discovery: who to talk to, what to watch, which questions surface the real problem, and how to write a problem statement the client agrees with before you propose any solution.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The craft of discovery: who to talk to, what to watch, which questions surface the real problem, and how to write a problem statement the client agrees with before you propose any solution.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Testing once and calling it verified is enough
Leave the quality check to the agent's memory so it improvises each week
Verify the result by reading it back in the system and comparing it to the source, the way the client's team would use it
Trust the agent's arithmetic because the tool call looked clean
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the second tier of proof: verify the result in the system against the source rather than trusting the agent's report.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
Here is a practical filter you can run against any request before you commit.
Here is not a practical filter you can run against any request before you commit.
questions.explanation: Here is a practical filter you can run against any request before you commit.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A system that runs on your personal API key is fine if it is well documented
The handover is verified when a competent client team member runs the system using only the documents and does not ask you a question
Secrets belong in the documentation so the client knows the values
Credentials should be transferred on the last day in a panic
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a handover is verified the same way a build is, once it survives a stranger using it without your help.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A green dashboard is the same as observability
Checking only the star job is sufficient since the others rarely drift
Relying on memory to run the fleet check is reliable
Check the whole fleet on a schedule of your own, and sample the actual output because no status system can catch stale content
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that you check the whole fleet on your own schedule and sample the substance of output, because a status screen will not tell you the numbers are stale.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Consulting Engagement Lifecycle”, what is the central focus?
options: The five-phase arc that every engagement runs: discover, design, implement, handover, support. What each phase produces, the exit test that lets you leave it, and where engagements quietly die.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The five-phase arc that every engagement runs: discover, design, implement, handover, support. What each phase produces, the exit test that lets you leave it, and where engagements quietly die.

questions.question: Per the lesson about documentation and handover, what is the central focus?
options: Making the client self-sufficient by naming an owner, building three document types, testing them live, and moving ownership
A tutorial on wiki software
A review of unrelated chat tools
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a handover is the transfer of ownership and operating knowledge so the client can run, maintain, and change the system without you.

questions.question: Per the lesson “When an Agent Is the Right Tool, and When to Say No”, what is the central focus?
options: The honest consultant's rule: an agent is not always the right answer, and the consultant who can say no protects both the client's money and their own reputation.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The honest consultant's rule: an agent is not always the right answer, and the consultant who can say no protects both the client's money and their own reputation. How to tell the work an agent should do from the work it should never touch, and how to walk away cleanly.

questions.question: Per the lesson about packaging reusable skills, what is the central focus?
options: Capturing what you built as a reusable skill written to travel to the next client without leaking the last one
A tutorial on documentation tools
A review of unrelated project software
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the discipline of turning the reusable core of a solved problem into an asset that makes the next delivery cheaper and lower risk.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Verification is optional if the agent completed its run
The system should refuse to mark a task complete only when there is a commit
A claim is finished only when it is verified, and it works here is the proof is a status while it should work is intent
Finishing means leaving without capturing what you learned
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that verification is the finish line and the proof is the actual tool output, not the agent's description of its own work.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: On native Windows it is not the PowerShell equivalent.
On native Windows it is the PowerShell equivalent.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
questions.explanation: On native Windows it is the PowerShell equivalent.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: These are the questions that separate discovery from a pleasant chat.
These is not the questions that separate discovery from a pleasant chat.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
questions.explanation: These are the questions that separate discovery from a pleasant chat.

questions.question: Per the lesson about estimation, what is the central focus?
options: A history of project management software
A review of unrelated scheduling tools
A summary of finance policy
Estimation as a sizing decision that produces a task you can start, complete, and verify in one focused window
questions.explanation: The lesson reframes estimation from predicting the future to deciding how you will work right now, optimizing for a shape of work you can actually complete.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Started is as good as done if the worker produced output
A running worker must close its task with a terminal call, either completing with proof or blocking with a clear reason
Shared decisions can be left for workers to coordinate among themselves
A handoff does not need to state how the work was verified
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that done is proven, not stated, so the worker must complete with proof or block with a clear reason and may not exit without one.
